part2.intro: Three young people write about a meal they will never forget.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Oliver
texts.text: Last spring I went camping in the mountains with my Scout group. On the first evening we cooked sausages and potatoes on a fire. Then it started to rain really hard, so we had to eat our dinner inside our small tents. The potatoes got cold and my plate was full of water, but it was still the best meal I've ever had. Everyone was laughing and singing all evening.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Mei
texts.text: For my grandmother's eightieth birthday, thirty people from our family had dinner at a Chinese restaurant. We ate roast duck, fish, rice and lots of vegetables. While we were eating, a young waiter dropped a bowl of soup on my uncle's head! For a moment everyone was quiet, but then my uncle started laughing, and so did everyone else. Grandma says it was her favourite birthday ever.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Carlos
texts.text: Last month it was my parents' wedding anniversary, so I decided to make them breakfast in bed as a present. It was the first time I cooked alone. I made omelettes with cheese and onion, orange juice and toast. Unfortunately, I forgot about the toast and it burned, so the kitchen smelled terrible. But my parents said it was the best breakfast they'd ever had.

items.q: Who cooked food on a fire?
Who made a meal as a present?
Who describes a funny accident?
Who had problems because of the weather?
Who ate with a very large group of relatives?
Who made a mistake while they were cooking?
Who ate with people who are not their family?

part3.title: The girl who grows her own lunch
part3.text:
Twelve-year-old Ava Morris eats salad every day – and she grows most of it herself.

It all started two years ago, when Ava's class visited a farm. "I couldn't believe how different a tomato tastes when you take it straight from the plant," she says. "The tomatoes in the supermarket taste of nothing!" When she got home, she asked her parents if she could grow some vegetables in the garden. "Dad said yes, but only if I looked after them myself."

Now Ava grows tomatoes, carrots, potatoes, onions and lettuce, and she has three apple trees too. She works in her garden for about an hour every day after school. "At weekends I spend even longer there," she says. "Some of my friends think it's boring, but I find it relaxing."

Last year, Ava had so many vegetables that her family couldn't eat them all. So she gave some to her neighbours, and they gave her eggs and homemade jam back. Then the head teacher heard about her garden and asked if she could help to start one at school.

The school garden opened in March. Thirty students now help Ava, and the school cook uses their vegetables in the soup and salads at lunchtime. "The best thing is that kids who never ate vegetables now try them," Ava says. "If you grow something yourself, you want to eat it!"

Ava's next plan? "I'd like to keep chickens," she says. "Mum isn't sure yet, but I'm working on it!"

part4.title: Chocolate
part4.text:
Most people love chocolate, but did you know that it comes from a tree? Chocolate is made from the beans of the cacao tree, which {19} in hot countries in Central and South America and West Africa.

More than 3,000 years ago, people in Mexico made a drink from cacao beans. It wasn't sweet like the chocolate we eat today, and they often {20} pepper to it! In the 1500s, Spanish travellers {21} cacao beans back to Europe. People there put sugar and milk in the drink, and it became very popular.

The first chocolate bar was made in England in 1847. {22} then, chocolate has become one of the most popular sweets in the world. People in Switzerland eat the {23} chocolate – about nine kilos each every year!

Doctors say a little dark chocolate can be good for you. But it has a lot of sugar and fat, so it's best to eat it only {24}.

items.q: What does the girl want to drink?

script.t: Hello. What would you like to drink? We've got tea, coffee, milk…
Have you got any orange juice?
Sorry, there isn't any today. But we've got lemonade.
Lovely, I'll have a glass of lemonade, please. And my mum would like a cup of tea.

items.q: Where is the bread?

script.t: Mum, where's the bread? It isn't on the table.
I put it in the fridge, so it stays fresh.
I've looked in the fridge. There's only butter and cheese.
Oh, sorry, I remember now. It's in the cupboard next to the cooker.

items.q: What time does the café close?

script.t: Let's go to the café after school. What time does it close?
In winter it closes at five, but in summer it stays open until six.
It's June now, so that's OK.
Yes, and school finishes at half past three, so we'll have lots of time.

items.q: What is the boy's favourite vegetable?

script.t: Do you like carrots, Dan?
They're OK, but I don't love them. And everyone thinks I like potatoes, because I eat so many chips!
So what's your favourite?
Onions. I know it's strange, but I love them – fried, in soup, in salad, anything.

items.q: What did the girl buy at the market?

script.t: What did you get at the market? Apples?
No, the apples looked a bit old. I wanted bananas, but there weren't any left.
So you didn't buy any fruit?
Yes, I did. I got some grapes. They're really sweet.
Great, I love grapes.

part2.intro: You will hear a teacher telling students about a school food fair.
part2.title: Year 8 Food Fair

items.label: Prize: a visit to a chocolate

script.t: Hello, Year 8! I'm here to tell you about this year's Food Fair. It's on Saturday the twenty-first of June – not the fourteenth, as we said in the school newsletter. Last year we had it in the school hall, but it was too hot and crowded, so this year it'll be outside in the school garden. If it rains, we'll move to the sports centre. Each class will have a stall and sell food from a different country. You can make pizza, pasta, curry, soup – anything you like! Students can come in free, but parents and other adults need a ticket. It costs three pounds, and children under five are free too. All the money will go to the children's hospital. There will also be a prize for the best stall. Last year the winners got cinema tickets, but this year the prize is a visit to a chocolate factory! I'm sure you'll all want to win that. If you have any questions, please talk to Miss Quinn. That's Q-U-I-N-N. She's the new cookery teacher, and you can find her in Room nine at lunchtime.

part3.intro: You will hear Ruby talking to her friend Ben about his weekend job at a café.

items.q: When does Ben work at the café?
Who owns the café?
What does Ben do at the café?
What does Ben enjoy most about the job?
What is Ben going to buy with his money?

script.t: Hi Ben! I saw you in the Corner Café on Sunday. Are you working there?
Hi Ruby. Yes, I started last month. I work every Sunday morning, from eight until twelve. I wanted to work on Saturdays too, but I've got football practice then.
Cool. How did you get the job?
My uncle owns the café. My neighbour worked there before, but she's gone to university, so my uncle asked me.
Do you cook? You make great pancakes!
Ha! No, the cook doesn't let anyone into the kitchen except to wash up. That's my job – I wash all the plates, cups and glasses. Sometimes I make drinks when it's busy, but not usually.
That sounds like hard work. Do you like it?

Yes. The money's OK, and I get a free breakfast, which is nice. But the best thing is the people. Lots of old people come in every week and they always talk to me. One man tells me about his travels around the world.
That's nice. What are you going to do with your money? Buy a new phone?
My phone's fine. I thought about getting a new bike, but my dad says I can have his old one. So I'm saving for a guitar. I want to start lessons in the summer.
Great idea!

script.t: Remember, it's going to be very hot tomorrow, so bring lots of water – at least two bottles. Don't bring sweets or chocolate. Bring healthy food like fruit, sandwiches and salad. items.intro: You will hear two friends talking about a new restaurant.
items.q: What do they agree about?

script.t: What did you think of the new Italian restaurant?
The pizza was amazing – the best I've ever had.
Me too. I loved it. But we waited a long time for the waiter, didn't we?
Did we? I didn't notice. And it was quite cheap, too.
Cheap? I thought it was really expensive!

items.intro: You will hear a man giving cooking instructions on the radio.
items.q: What is he explaining?

script.t: Today we're making something quick and easy. First, break three eggs into a bowl and add a little salt and pepper. Mix them well. Then cut an onion and a tomato into small pieces. Put a little oil in a frying pan and, when it's hot, add the eggs and the vegetables. Cook for three minutes, then put it on a plate. It's lovely with a green salad!

part5.intro: You will hear Lucy talking to her dad about a class picnic. What will each person bring?

script.t: So, Lucy, what's everyone bringing to the class picnic on Friday?
Well, I'm doing the sandwiches. I wanted to make chicken sandwiches, but some people don't eat meat, so I'm making cheese ones.
OK, I'll buy some cheese tomorrow. What about your friend Sam?
Sam's mum makes amazing pizza, so we asked him to bring some. But it's difficult to carry on the bus. So he's bringing drinks instead – two big bottles of lemonade.
Good. And your teacher? Is Mrs Hall bringing anything?
Yes. She's bringing all the plates and cups, because she doesn't want us to use glass.
Very sensible. And Hana?
Hana loves baking. She's making chocolate biscuits for everyone.
Lovely. What about Kevin?
Kevin said he'd bring water, but Mrs Hall said everyone should bring their own bottle of water. So he's bringing some apples from his grandparents' farm.
Good. His grandparents grow the best apples I've ever eaten. So, sandwiches, lemonade, plates and cups, biscuits and apples. Is anyone bringing a cake?
No, but there's a café in the park, so we can buy ice cream there if we're still hungry.
It sounds like a great picnic. Can I come too?
Sorry, Dad – no parents!
